measure: denial rate, conventional home-purchase loans (first lien, 1–4 family, owner-occupied)
statement: In 2023, Black applicants were denied conventional home-purchase loans 2.9× as often as non-Hispanic white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, "FFIEC Publishes 2023 Data on Mortgage Lending"
notes: Raw denial rates from HMDA. They do not control for income, debt or credit score. Comparison group: non-Hispanic white applicants.

measure: denial rate, conventional home-purchase loans (first lien, 1–4 family, owner-occupied)
statement: In 2023, Hispanic white applicants were denied conventional home-purchase loans 2.1× as often as non-Hispanic white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, "FFIEC Publishes 2023 Data on Mortgage Lending"
notes: Raw denial rates from HMDA. They do not control for income, debt or credit score. Comparison group: non-Hispanic white applicants. The source reports "Hispanic-White" applicants, not all Hispanic applicants.

measure: denial rate, conventional home-purchase loans (first lien, 1–4 family, owner-occupied)
statement: In 2023, Asian applicants were denied conventional home-purchase loans 1.6× as often as non-Hispanic white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, "FFIEC Publishes 2023 Data on Mortgage Lending"
notes: Raw denial rates from HMDA. They do not control for income, debt or credit score. Comparison group: non-Hispanic white applicants.

measure: median earnings for each $100 that men earn
statement: In 2025, women who worked full-time, year-round earned $83.90 for each $100 that men earned (median earnings).
source_title: U.S. Census Bureau, "Income in the United States: 2025" (P60-289)
notes: Female-to-male earnings ratio, Table 12. It was 80.6% in 2024. It compares medians and does not control for job or hours beyond full-time.

measure: gender classification error rate, IBM classifier
statement: IBM's face analysis tool got the gender of darker-skinned women wrong 34.7% of the time, and of lighter-skinned men 0.3% of the time.
source_title: Buolamwini, Joy, and Timnit Gebru, "Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification"
notes: IBM classifier, Table 4 (p. 9). Microsoft and Face++ showed the same pattern (20.8% vs 0.0%, 34.5% vs 0.8%). Year = publication year. "Darker" = Fitzpatrick skin types IV–VI, so it also includes some of our mid skin tones. This tests gender classification, not face recognition.

measure: average word error rate of 5 speech recognition systems
statement: Speech recognition systems from Amazon, Apple, Google, IBM and Microsoft got 35% of words wrong for Black speakers and 19% for white speakers.
source_title: Koenecke, Allison, et al., "Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition," PNAS
notes: 42 white and 73 Black speakers, matched on age and gender. Year = publication year; the systems were tested in 2019.

measure: callback rate for job applications (identical résumés)
statement: Résumés with Black-sounding names got a callback for an interview 0.67× as often as the same résumés with white-sounding names.
source_title: Bertrand, Marianne, and Sendhil Mullainathan, "Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination," NBER Working Paper 9873
notes: Field experiment, about 5,000 résumés to job ads in Boston and Chicago, 2001–2002. Table 1, all sent résumés. The published version (American Economic Review, 2004) reports 9.65% vs 6.45%.

statement: In 2024, Black women died of maternal causes 3.2× as often as white women (44.8 vs 14.2 deaths per 100,000 live births).
source_title: Hoyert, Donna L., "Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2024," NCHS Health E-Stats
notes: Maternal death = during pregnancy or within 42 days after it. Hispanic women: 12.1, Asian women: 18.1. The rate for Black women was 69.9 in 2021.

statement: In 2024, women age 40 and older died of maternal causes 3.8× as often as women age 25–39.
source_title: Hoyert, Donna L., "Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2024," NCHS Health E-Stats
notes: The source group is "40 and older"; the site tag is age:40s. Women younger than 25: 13.7. Older age is also a medical risk factor, so this gap is not only about care quality.

statement: When GPT-4 compared a résumé with the same résumé plus a disability-related award, scholarship, talk or membership, it showed prejudice against the version that mentioned disability.
source_title: Glazko, Kate, et al., "Identifying and Improving Disability Bias in GPT-Based Resume Screening," FAccT 2024
notes: Audit study with GPT-4. The résumé with disability items was ranked first in only 15 of 60 trials (Table, the text says 15/70). A custom GPT trained on disability justice principles reduced the bias.

measure: photos classified as the right gender, average of 4 commercial face analysis services
statement: Commercial face analysis tools classified photos of trans men as men 70.5% of the time, and photos of men 97.6% of the time.
source_title: Scheuerman, Morgan Klaus, Jacob M. Paul, and Jed R. Brubaker, "How Computers See Gender: An Evaluation of Gender Classification in Commercial Facial Analysis and Image Labeling Services," CSCW 2019
notes: Table 3 (PDF p. 14), text p. 15. 350 Instagram photos for each hashtag. The paper notes that it cannot know if the people in #man are cisgender.

measure: photos classified as the right gender, average of 4 commercial face analysis services
statement: Commercial face analysis tools classified photos of trans women as women 87.3% of the time, and photos of women 98.3% of the time.
source_title: Scheuerman, Morgan Klaus, Jacob M. Paul, and Jed R. Brubaker, "How Computers See Gender: An Evaluation of Gender Classification in Commercial Facial Analysis and Image Labeling Services," CSCW 2019
notes: Table 3 (PDF p. 14), text p. 15. 350 Instagram photos for each hashtag.

statement: Commercial face analysis tools can only label a face as male or female, so they can never classify a nonbinary person correctly.
source_title: Scheuerman, Morgan Klaus, Jacob M. Paul, and Jed R. Brubaker, "How Computers See Gender: An Evaluation of Gender Classification in Commercial Facial Analysis and Image Labeling Services," CSCW 2019
notes: The authors set the accuracy for #agender, #genderqueer and #nonbinary to 0% because no correct answer is possible (PDF p. 14). It is a missing category, not a measurement.

group: Deaf and hard of hearing speakers
measure: word error rate, average of 4 speech recognition systems (incl. OpenAI Whisper)
statement: Speech recognition systems got 52.6% of words wrong for deaf and hard of hearing speakers, and 5.0% for hearing speakers.
source_title: Zhao, Robin, Anna S.G. Choi, Allison Koenecke, and Anaïs Rameau, "Quantification of Automatic Speech Recognition System Performance on d/Deaf and Hard of Hearing Speech," The Laryngoscope
notes: Abstract and Table II. Small sample: 24 deaf or hard of hearing and 9 hearing speakers. Speakers who mainly use sign language: 70.2% errors; oral speakers only: 19.7%.

measure: word error rate, average of 5 speech recognition systems
statement: Speech recognition systems got 41% of words wrong for Black men, and 21% for white men.
source_title: Koenecke, Allison, et al., "Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition," PNAS
notes: Results section (0.41 vs 0.21). Systems tested in 2019.

measure: word error rate, average of 5 speech recognition systems
statement: Speech recognition systems got 30% of words wrong for Black women, and 17% for white women.
source_title: Koenecke, Allison, et al., "Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition," PNAS
notes: Results section (0.30 vs 0.17). Systems tested in 2019.

measure: language models choosing the death sentence in a hypothetical murder trial
statement: When language models judged a hypothetical murder case, they chose the death sentence 27.7% of the time for a speaker of African American English, and 22.8% for a speaker of Standard American English.
source_title: Hofmann, Valentin, Pratyusha Ria Kalluri, Dan Jurafsky, and Sharese King, "AI Generates Covertly Racist Decisions about People Based on Their Dialect," Nature
notes: Nature p. 150, Fig. 3c. The text said the same thing in two dialects; race was never named. Convictions: 68.7% vs 62.1%. Hypothetical decisions, not real courts.

measure: false matches per 100,000 comparisons, face recognition algorithm imperial_002
statement: One face recognition algorithm wrongly matched two different Vietnamese-born people about 50× as often as two different Polish-born people.
source_title: Grother, Patrick, Mei Ngan, and Kayee Hanaoka, "Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 3: Demographic Effects," NISTIR 8280
notes: PDF p. 34: false match rate 0.0024 (Vietnam) vs 0.000046 (Poland), same sex and country, any age. One algorithm only; country of birth is the report's proxy for race. NIST also found 2–5× more false matches for women than men, and the highest rates for people 65 and older.

measure: GPT-3.5 ranked the résumé first out of 8 equal résumés (financial analyst job)
statement: When GPT-3.5 ranked 8 equally qualified résumés for a financial analyst job, it put the one with a Black man's name first 7.6% of the time, and the one with a white man's name 12.1% of the time.
source_title: Yin, Leon, Davey Alba, and Leonardo Nicoletti, "OpenAI's GPT Is a Recruiter's Dream Tool. Tests Show There's Racial Bias," Bloomberg (data on GitHub)
notes: From the authors' data file (performance ranking CSV). With no bias, each group would be first 12.5% of the time. One job and one model; results differ by job.

statement: Face recognition algorithms wrongly matched older people more often than middle-aged adults. For women, people 65 and older had the highest false match rates.
source_title: Grother, Patrick, Mei Ngan, and Kayee Hanaoka, "Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 3: Demographic Effects," NISTIR 8280
notes: PDF p. 5 and p. 54. The numbers are only in heatmap figures, so this is a finding.
